item.title: Should Travelers Give Up on Summer in Western Europe?
item.description:
Nearly every year since 2000, Jenise Campbell, 54, has traveled to Paris from New York. Last year marked her first summer visit and it went so well that she went again this year. She arrived in late June, with plans to stay until mid-August, but after three weeks, she did something she described as “unthinkable”: She changed her flight and went home.

Her reason for absconding? The extreme heat.

“I would never, ever leave Paris early, but walking around with your pants stuck to you,” Ms. Campbell said, “I just thought: ‘There’s no way I’m doing this.’”

On the heels of the third heat wave in Western Europe since May, some travelers are starting to question whether taking a summer vacation in Europe is a good idea.

The recent heat waves have sent temperatures above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in Paris; to 111 degrees Fahrenheit in Valencia, Spain; and over 100 in Geneva. London sweltered in the mid-90s as early as May. Dry conditions also contributed to fires: One, about 60 miles from Madrid, has been raging for days.

Experts said that while temperatures are finally cooling, they will likely rise again in the coming weeks. “Visitors to Western Europe should plan for hot spells to keep returning in waves through August,” said Dominik Jung, a meteorologist in Germany.

As they have the last few summers, travelers, residents and local officials searched for ways to cope. In Rome, misting fans and cooling stations were set up outside the Colosseum. In Paris, the Canal St.-Martin was opened earlier than planned for swimming, while in London, people struggled to secure spots at crowded pools. Some museums limited their hours, because they couldn’t keep their galleries cool enough, including the Louvre. “Heat buildup is greatest toward the end of the day and is further intensified by high visitor numbers,” the museum said in a statement.

The heat has also made it clear to some travelers and those working in tourism that air conditioning may now be nonnegotiable.

Ms. Campbell, the repeat traveler from New York, said that while she’s used to the heat in Manhattan, there was something “different and hotter” about the temperatures in Paris. During her stay, she said it got so “unbearable” that she spent much of the day in her air-conditioned hotel room, only leaving to explore before 11 a.m. or after 6 p.m.

“For U.S. travelers, air conditioning is an expectation, but this summer they’re finding out it’s not a given in much of Europe,” said Melanie Fish, the vice president of public relations at Expedia Group.

Among Americans, searches in Europe using the “air-conditioned” filter on Hotels.com, which is owned by Expedia Group, jumped about 700 percent during the July 2-to-July 15 period compared with searches for summer accommodations made three months earlier.

Travelers weren’t just looking for air conditioning: Some were looking to leave the hottest cities altogether, Ms. Fish said. “American travelers are seeking cooler European destinations to escape the heat, with searches up for Copenhagen, Denmark, almost 500 percent, and Reykjavik, Iceland, almost 200 percent.”

Sam Randall, an Airbnb representative, said that since mid-June, searches for air-conditioned accommodations in France were up 88 percent, and those for beach access jumped by 86 percent. “Amenities that help cope with heat are in particularly high demand,” he said.

Victoria Faucanie, the chief marketing officer for Beaumarly, a Paris-based restaurant, hotel and club group, said that when her company bought the building housing the restaurant Café Français over a decade ago, one dining room had air conditioning but the other did not. At the time, it wasn’t an issue because temperatures weren’t as high as frequently or as persistently as they are now.

“With this high temperature now, we are closing half of the restaurant, so we are losing a lot of money,” Ms. Faucanie said. “We realized that we need to have AC everywhere.” She added that the restaurant is in talks to have it next year.

Paige Dacanay, 31, visiting Madrid from San Diego for the summer, said she doesn’t leave her rental apartment without two fans — one electric and one hand fan — and on the hottest days, she has taken up to three cold showers. “I was expecting not to have a ton of AC, but actually living here without it is extremely humbling,” she said. “You just have to get comfortable being hot.”

Renske Schuitmaker, 34, visited her home country, the Netherlands, from Nairobi during the late June heat wave. Ms. Schuitmaker, who was pregnant during her trip, said she had to leave her rental and stay with relatives who had air conditioning in Amsterdam, where temperatures got well into the 90s. Dutch authorities said that across the Netherlands, where air conditioning is uncommon, the June heat wave caused around 480 deaths.

Pamela Minucci, 64, and Robert Wilson, 65, who were visiting London from Connecticut for their daughter’s wedding, found themselves looking for places to sit in the shade. At one point, the couple sat at an air-conditioned pub showing a cricket match for hours. Asked if they followed the sport, Mr. Wilson chuckled. “We did that day,” he said.

Even air-conditioned hotels are trying to figure out new ways to keep guests entertained and cool. In Florence, Italy, guests at the Hotel Savoy, part of the Rocco Forte group, have private access to a pool at a “Medici residence nestled along the banks of the Arno River,” said Gaia Cavazzoni, the hotel’s assistant public relations manager. The hotel is also offering guests night tours through the Uffizi Galleries, after temperatures have dropped.

Papa Gyimah, 38, who was visiting Paris from Ghana, said he has been visiting France during the summer for years, but will now look to come in the spring or fall, when temperatures will likely be cooler. “Each year, it gets more difficult to walk around,” Mr. Gyimah said about his recent summers in France. “You’re always thirsty, you have to slow down and even if you get on public transport, it’s suffocating.”

Ms. Campbell has also changed her mind: She plans to return to Paris in September, but won’t visit the city in the summer going forward.

But Ms. Dacanay in Spain is not deterred. Instead, she will just stay somewhere with air conditioning. “Nothing will keep me away from a Euro summer,” she said.

On the heels of three heat waves, some travelers are starting to change their minds about visiting Western Europe in the summer. Have you thought about rescheduling your European vacation to a different time of year because of the heat?

@Tariro MzezewaWe had tickets to Portugal for August 🇵🇹 — we’d planned on 30 days to celebrate our 30th anniversary. We cancelled them and will plan to go next spring. I’m disappointed to miss the eclipse, though. We’ll do something local on our actual anniversary, maybe go to New York, see a couple shows, museums, eat some food— and if it’s not 100 degrees or drenching windswept rain, walk the city (one of our favorite things to do).

@Tariro Mzezewa - I usually do a perennial European trip in late Spring. This year I went to Clermont-Ferrand, central France, in mid June with intentions to bicycle. The first two days of distance riding were so hot I was overwhelmed. I drank four to six liters of water daily. My AirBnB did not have air conditioning so even with cool showers my body temperature remains challenged by the environment 24 hours constantly. It took about two additional days of rest to have my sixty four year old body revert to a normal hydrated, proper temperature state from the overheated activity. I will adjust France/ Spain to April and May in coming years.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: Chaos Breaks Out at Border Crossings With Iraq
item.description:
Two of Iraq’s border crossings were attacked on Thursday during the latest round of hostilities overnight in the Middle East, according to officials and videos on social media verified by The New York Times. It was not immediately clear who launched the attacks.

The first attack occurred in the early morning hours of Thursday near the Iranian side of the Shalamcheh border crossing with Iraq in Iran’s Khuzestan province. Iranian and Iraqi media outlets reported that a rest station for police officers at the crossing had been struck by U.S. airstrikes.

U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the region, did not immediately respond to questions about the attack.

In a video, crowds can be seen fleeing as explosions ring out near the Iranian side of the crossing.

The footage, which circulated online early Thursday morning, shows people carrying suitcases and rucksacks running away from a blaze. The attacks killed two people, according to Iranian officials.

Additional footage of the aftermath, also verified by The Times, shows a damaged telecommunications tower inside a small compound within the border crossing facility.

The footage emerged shortly before U.S. Central Command said in a statement that it had completed its 12th consecutive night of strikes against Iranian military sites. The statement did not mention targeting of a border crossing facility.

In what appeared to be a retaliatory strike, the Abdali border crossing between Kuwait and Iraq was also hit on Thursday afternoon.

Gen. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi, a spokesman for Kuwait’s defense ministry, said in a statement that the crossing had come “under attack by hostile drones,” without specifying their origin, and that there had been no casualties. Since the war began in late February, Iran has launched missile and drone attacks at Kuwait as well as other nations in the Middle East, saying it is targeting U.S. military installations there.

The spokesman said in a second statement that the border crossing was also subjected to “repeated” attacks Thursday evening, but that no injuries were reported.

Videos verified by The Times showed dark clouds of smoke rising on the Kuwaiti side of the border crossing near a radio tower and billowing over several curved metal structures.

Another video verified by The Times shows multiple cars and trucks parked on the side of the road on the Iraqi side of the border, with people filming as clouds of smoke continue to emanate from the area.

Neither Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps nor U.S. Central Command has commented on the attack.

The Iraqi government has not commented on either attack.

item.title: The Tate Brothers, in Federal Custody, Watch Their Powerful Backers Go Quiet
item.description:
On Sunday morning, hours after the manosphere influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested by federal agents in Miami, one of their representatives reached out to Alina Habba.

Not long ago, Ms. Habba, a lawyer, was a vocal supporter of the Tate brothers as they faced allegations of human trafficking and other serious crimes in Romania and Britain. In a podcast appearance in January 2025, shortly after being named a counselor to President Trump, she told Andrew Tate, “I got your back over here.”

Now the brothers were in a federal detention center after Britain requested their extradition for a slew of new criminal charges there. Their representative wanted to know: Was Ms. Habba free to talk?

She did not respond, according to two people familiar with the outreach. It was a sign of the brothers’ eroding support among their onetime allies on the American right.

In recent years, the Tates had leveraged their enormous following of young men to cultivate support among Mr. Trump’s advisers, family members and other prominent conservatives. Those efforts paid off last year when, feeling pressure from members of the new Trump administration, Romanian prosecutors lifted a travel ban on the brothers, freeing them to leave the country and jet-set around the world.

But they are now facing a new level of legal jeopardy. Britain has issued 38 charges against them, including rape and sex trafficking; Andrew Tate was also charged with extreme pornography and indecent images of children. The brothers have denied all of the criminal accusations and called the charges politically motivated.

The extradition request has forced the Trump administration to participate in the process: Federal prosecutors are representing the British government’s case in a Miami court.

Mr. Trump does not plan to intervene in the case, said the White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, on Thursday. And many of the Tates’ allies in the president’s orbit, who were once happy to be associated with their brand of hyper-masculinity, now appear to be backing away.

Ms. Habba, who is no longer in the administration but still speaks with Mr. Trump, wants nothing to do with the Tates, according to people familiar with her thinking.

Paul Ingrassia, the acting general counsel of the General Services Administration, who previously served on the Tates’ legal team and has lavished praise on Andrew, wrote a post on X shortly after the arrests criticizing “politically driven prosecutions.” In a call with The New York Times on Thursday, Mr. Ingrassia said the post was simply articulating his beliefs about the Constitution.

Asked if he still supported the Tates, he said, “I have no ongoing connection to them now.”

Donald Trump Jr., who once called Andrew Tate a friend and publicly defended him against previous criminal allegations, has said nothing about the arrests. Neither has his younger brother Barron Trump, who had also been friendly with Andrew. Candace Owens, a conservative commentator who backed both brothers on her popular show, has also stayed silent.

Privately, people close to Donald Jr. have played down his relationship with the Tates; one person said he had not spoken with anyone in the administration about their arrests.

Asked by The Times about his retweeting of Tristan Tate on Saturday, Roger Stone, a prominent Republican operative, said he did so before the news of their arrests. And Paolo Zampolli, a special envoy for Mr. Trump who had hosted the Tates at a party in Washington two days before the arrests, said he hadn’t realized the extent of the allegations against them.

“I didn’t know they were arrest material,” Mr. Zampolli said in an interview.

Not everyone is pulling back from the brothers. Representative Abe Hamadeh, Republican of Arizona, spoke out against their extradition, writing on social media that “political lawfare is dangerous.”

The conservative media star Tucker Carlson, who has conducted sympathetic interviews of the Tates, told The Times, without evidence, that he believed their arrests were related to their outspoken criticism of Israel.

“After decades of ignoring grooming gangs and covering for Jeffrey Epstein, the British and American governments seemed to have lost interest in prosecuting sex crimes,” Mr. Carlson said. “Then the Tate brothers criticized Israel, and I was reminded that under certain circumstances they’re willing to act.”

Joseph McBride, a longtime lawyer for the Tates, disputed that their support had eroded. He said he was not surprised that any Trump official who had previously backed the brothers was now taking a more neutral stance given the administration’s role in the legal case.

Mr. McBride said the Tates were focused on fighting the extradition request in court rather than seeking help from Mr. Trump’s circle. He said he was unaware that a representative for the Tates had contacted Ms. Habba.

“There’s no reason at this point for Trump to parachute in from Air Force One to the courtroom, because we think we’ll win in court,” Mr. McBride said.

In recent years, there has been only one instance in which the United States has refused an extradition request from Britain.

The Tates, who have American and British citizenship, made their fortunes by running an online pornography business, first in Britain and then Romania, and by selling online courses to young men. One offering was called P.H.D., for “Pimping Hoes Degree.”

Romania began its investigation into the brothers in 2022. Two years later, prosecutors in Britain charged the brothers with rape, sexual assault and human trafficking. The two countries agreed that Britain would wait to extradite the Tates until the Romanian criminal investigation was done, but that case has suffered major setbacks.

Since their release from Romania in February 2025, the Tates had been living large, spending time in the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan, Hong Kong and Russia. During a January visit to Miami, they made headlines when a video circulated of them partying at a club with Nicholas J. Fuentes and other far-right influencers while the song “Heil Hitler” by the rapper formerly known as Kanye West blasted from speakers.

They did not go to Britain, where they faced not only the 2024 criminal charges but continuing investigations into other accusations.

In March, a police watchdog group said it was reviewing potential misconduct by the officers who had originally investigated rape and sexual assault allegations against Andrew Tate from 2015. Shortly after, the British police reopened that investigation.

Last year, after the Tates visited Florida, the state’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, opened an investigation of the brothers. His office also sent an email to Matthew Jury, a lawyer who represents several Tate accusers in Britain, promising to assist if Britain ordered their extradition, as first reported by The Times of London.

Mr. Jury’s law firm passed the message onto the home secretary through an intermediary but did not receive a response, according to a person familiar with the communication. As recently as June, the firm wrote letters to Prime Minister Keir Starmer criticizing the government’s inaction over extradition, according to The Telegraph.

That month, prosecutors in Britain, including one who specializes in cases involving child sexual images, successfully fought an effort by the brothers asking the court to disclose the names of the women in the original criminal charges.

The Tates were arrested on Saturday evening as they arrived at a bare-knuckle-boxing event that Andrew was supposed to co-host. British prosecutors said the charges stemmed from incidents that happened between July 2010 and August 2017 but did not disclose names or other identifying details.

In the days before the arrests, the brothers had been posting on social media from Washington, where they were photographed with Representative Wesley Hunt, Republican of Texas, and partied with Mr. Zampolli.

Mr. McBride said in a statement on Saturday that the extradition request was approved by a “low-level functionary at the Justice Department who never got approval from leadership.” But higher-ups in the agency did sign off on the arrests, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss it.

The Tates will remain behind bars in Florida as a federal judge considers whether Britain has met the legal threshold for extradition, a process that could take months. If the judge signs off on the extradition request, it will then go to Secretary of State Marco Rubio for final approval.

Asked about the request while traveling in Manila on Wednesday, Mr. Rubio said that while the matter is considered by the judge, “there’s no role for us to play at this moment or maybe ever.”

Lauren Southern, a former conservative influencer who has accused Andrew Tate of raping her in Romania and provided testimony to Romanian authorities, was among those who celebrated news of the extradition request.

“It’s been a really wonderful weekend for those of us who are rooting for justice,” she told The Times. “Now there’s a reckoning and suddenly everyone wants to pretend they had nothing to do with building this beast.”

It is unclear where the Romanian criminal case against the brothers is headed and how it may be affected by the extradition request. The country’s foreign minister said she had not been informed about it ahead of time. A spokeswoman for Romanian prosecutors did not comment.

The Trump administration’s willingness to honor the request is fueling rifts on the American right, as Mr. Carlson, Mr. Fuentes and others seek to frame it within broader political talking points. More traditional conservatives, like Ben Shapiro, are accusing the Tates’ allies of embracing misogyny and criminal behavior.

“The conservative movement should cast them aside now, just as it should have years ago,” Mr. Shapiro told The Times.

Reporting was contributed by Michael Crowley, Shawn McCreesh, David Ovalle and Ed Wong.

item.title: Trump Throws a Potential Wrench in the Saudi Nuclear Deal He Just Inked
item.description:
President Trump’s insistence on Thursday that Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel as a condition of its nuclear deal with the United States, which was already signed, puts Saudi officials in an extremely awkward position.

Saudi Arabia has its own condition for normalization of relations with Israel, which it has long insisted on — a pathway toward a Palestinian state. And in the hours after Mr. Trump’s sudden announcement, there has been resounding silence from the kingdom.

“I don’t think the Saudis want to give this air,” said Rosemary Kelanic, director of the Middle East program at Defense Priorities, a Washington research group. “They want it to quietly go away.”

Israel is extremely unpopular in Saudi Arabia, particularly over its handling of the war in Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023, attack led by Hamas. Israel’s military activity in the territory and the Israeli government’s resistance to the creation of a Palestinian state make agreeing to Mr. Trump’s condition “so politically toxic, it could jeopardize the survival of the Saudi regime,” Ms. Kelanic said.

Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s crown prince, is not an elected leader, but he does need popular support, she said. Agreeing to Mr. Trump’s condition, she added, “would poison the legitimacy of his government.”

Saudi Arabia is now in a bind, analysts said, assuming Mr. Trump meant what he said — which may not necessarily be the case. The terms of the agreement have not been released, and Mr. Trump has frequently used social media posts and other statements as a negotiating tool even after deals have ostensibly been sealed.

Analysts said the deal could still move forward, given the uncertainty about Mr. Trump’s demand.

“We don’t know if this is just a transitory reaction or a serious condition,” said Aaron David Miller, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and a former negotiator and adviser on Middle East policy at the State Department.

The nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia sparked criticism in Israel and beyond — including from The Wall Street Journal editorial board, Mr. Miller noted — and he said that the president may be responding to critics who say that he has relinquished leverage over the kingdom by moving forward with the agreement.

Mr. Miller also doubted that Saudi Arabia would be willing to agree to Mr. Trump’s new demand. At this point, he said, getting Saudi Arabia on board with normalizing relations with Israel’s current government is not even a “thought experiment.”

Both analysts agreed that Mr. Trump’s unpredictable approach to international diplomacy could also mean that the deal proceeds without any apparent alteration.

Saudi officials “have good reason to think he might tweet something totally different” about the agreement later, Ms. Kelanic said. And, she added, whatever he posts about the agreement “doesn’t change the content of the deal.”

item.title: Strikes Against Saudi Tankers in the Red Sea Send Oil Past $100 a Barrel
item.description:
The price of oil hit $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May after militants allied with Iran said they had hit two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, stoking fears that another crucial shipping route may be choked off with a cascade of consequences for the global economy.

President Trump said he would hold Iran responsible for any further attacks by the Houthi militants, who control much of Yemen. He also threatened to expand the war to include the group itself. The warning came after the United States and Iran traded strikes across the Middle East for a 12th consecutive night.

The maritime strikes claimed by the Houthis’ were the first since the group announced a blockade on Saudi vessels earlier this week.

If the Houthis hit any more ships, Mr. Trump wrote in his post, “major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves, who I am very disappointed with in that they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart.”

With the cease-fire between Iran and the United States in tatters, Democrats and a handful of Republicans in the House of Representatives on Thursday voted for a second time to demand that Mr. Trump seek Congressional authorization to keep U.S. troops engaged in the war. The president effectively ignored a similar rebuke last month. The Senate voted 49 to 47 against taking up its own war powers resolution.

When the United States and Iran reached a deal in June to cease hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices plummeted to prewar levels. Countries that rely on Middle Eastern supplies relished a reprieve from a crisis that forced the cancellation of thousands of flights and ate into the budgets of hundreds of millions of people. Farmers who use diesel fuel for irrigation and machinery as well as petrochemical products like fertilizer were especially hurt.

“Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!” Mr. Trump declared when the deal was announced.

The collapse of the cease-fire earlier this month and the resumption of daily airstrikes had already put oil-importing countries back into crisis mode. Now the entry of Houthi militants into the war, and their attacks on ships using another critical waterway, has deepened the oil shock by cutting off another shipping route to Asia.

The war in Ukraine has also contributed to the oil market turmoil, disrupting shipments in the Black Sea as well as fuel production at Russian refineries.

U.S. stock markets opened sharply lower on Thursday. And the yield on the 10-year treasury bond, a key indicator that influences mortgage and student loan rates, jumped past 4.7 percent, its highest level in many months.

The European Central Bank, which last month became the first major central bank to raise interest rates in response to the war with Iran, held them steady at a meeting on Thursday. But the head of the bank, Christine Lagarde, told reporters that “uncertainty remains high.”

The Houthi attacks raise the prospect of wider economic turmoil, especially in the shipping business.

Some ships bound for Asia this week have been forced to embark on lengthy detours through the Suez Canal, the Mediterranean Sea and around the southern tip of Africa. The delays and added costs blunt the effectiveness of a pipeline that crosses the Arabian Peninsula, which Saudi Arabia has relied on heavily during the war as an alternate pathway for oil exports.

With the Persian Gulf largely closed off, oil prices are now 40 percent higher than they were before the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran in February. The average price of gasoline in the United States was $4.09 on Thursday, according to AAA, a 15-cent jump from a week earlier.

The Saudi authorities on Thursday confirmed a strike on one of its ships, the Encelia, without specifying the origin of the attack. It said that the crew was safe. The Saudis have not commented on the Houthi claim regarding a second ship.

Neither the United States nor Iran has signaled much appetite for a return to negotiations. In recent days, Iranian and American officials have instead vowed to respond to each other’s attacks with fresh ones of their own.

U.S. Central Command, which coordinates military operations in the Middle East, said it had launched a wave of strikes overnight to degrade Iran’s ability to threaten commercial shipping, targeting drone and missile storage sites and air defenses.

That language, which the U.S. military has employed on a daily basis, does not explicitly acknowledge U.S. strikes on infrastructure that can be used for civilian purposes, like roads and ports. Such attacks could be considered war crimes under international law.

Mr. Trump has threatened to attack a bridge or power plant “any time the Islamic republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz.”

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said overnight that it had launched attacks on U.S. military targets in Jordan and Kuwait, including a communications tower, accusing U.S. forces of attacking equivalent infrastructure in Iran.

Videos circulating on social media and verified by The New York Times showed two of Iraq’s border crossings attacked on Thursday, with people carrying suitcases fleeing the explosions.

The first attack occurred in the early hours of Thursday near the Iranian side of the Shalamcheh border crossing in Khuzestan Province. Iranian and Iraqi media outlets reported that a rest station for police officers at the crossing had been hit by U.S. airstrikes. U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to questions about the attack.

Additional footage showed a damaged telecommunications tower inside a small compound within the border crossing facility.

In what appeared to be a retaliatory strike, the Abdali border crossing between Kuwait and Iraq was also hit on Thursday afternoon.

Gen. Saud Abdulaziz al-Otaibi, a spokesman for Kuwait’s defense ministry, said in a statement that the crossing had come “under attack by hostile drones,” without specifying their origin, and that there had been no casualties.

Reporting was contributed by Shirin Hakim, Robert Jimison, James McManagan, Sanjana Varghese, Aruni Soni and Euan Ward.

item.title: The Defining Image of India’s Gen Z Protests
item.description:
The 27-year-old woman stood alone in front of a police van, hand pressed to the hood, and refused to let it pass until officers released the protesters detained inside.

“It was one girl fighting the system,” said Sohit Mishra, a 33-year-old journalist who is covering the burst of student protests in India. He captured video of the standoff on Wednesday, as rain lashed the busy Mumbai street. After about 15 minutes, he said, amid the honking of cars and the cries of people surrounding the van, the police officers bowed to the woman’s demand and let the protesters go.

The video and photos of the woman, a model named Rhiya Ahir, have gone viral, viewed hundreds of thousands of times on social media, reflecting both how quickly a new protest movement is spreading across India and the resolve of the young people leading it.

“When I confronted them, I was shaking on the inside,” Ms. Ahir told local news media. But, she added, “I knew that what I was doing was right.”

Mr. Mishra said her actions helped unify the protesters, who have faced down a heavy police presence. “When they were released, the entire moment was so electric,” he said. “People were cheering, hugging each other.”

The demonstrations began in New Delhi, India’s capital, where thousands of people have gathered at a protest site near Parliament in recent days, returning even after police cracked down with force. In Mumbai, India’s financial capital, and Bengaluru, the country’s Silicon Valley, young people have staged smaller demonstrations.

By Thursday, the protests were beginning to reach across India, from Hyderabad and Chennai in the south to Lucknow and Jaipur in the north, as the country’s young people try to turn their cause into a nationwide movement. The Cockroach Janta Party, a movement that began as satire, taking its name from an insult, is organizing the protests and said they have reached 30 cities so far.

The C.J.P. has called for nationwide rallies on Friday.

The frustration powering the recent protests erupted in May after leaks of medical school entrance exams forced millions of students to retake their tests. The leaks have become emblematic of India’s troubled education system and the struggle among the country’s young people to find jobs. The movement has been fueled by a wider disaffection with what protesters say is a lack of government accountability for corruption and the mismanagement of the education system.

The protests are posing one of the most substantial challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his 12 years in power. On Thursday, Mr. Modi made his first direct reference to the protests, saying in a post on X that “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth!” and promised to fast-track punishments for the exam leakers.

The acknowledgment was rare for Mr. Modi, a strongman leader, and is a sign of the delicate balance he must find between placating young people, a significant voting bloc in India, and ensuring that his ruling party doesn’t look weak.

Many demonstrators say his response is insufficient. Their demands include structural change in education and jobs, as well as compensation for the protesters injured in clashes on Monday.

The protests in New Delhi and elsewhere have been going on for more than a month. But the C.J.P.’s call to march to Parliament on July 20, its first day in session, has given the movement momentum. Thousands of people gathered in the capital for the march, and many have remained camped out at the protest site for days despite authorities’ calls to disperse.

item.title: What to Know About Iran and the Houthis
item.description:
After months of relatively minimal involvement in the U.S.-Iran war, the Iranian-backed Houthi militant group in Yemen is making a delayed but potentially consequential entrance.

The Houthis claimed to have launched missile and drone strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea on Wednesday, just days after the group declared a naval blockade on shipping linked to Saudi Arabia.

The group has long portrayed itself as a frontline member of Iran’s so-called axis of resistance and has publicly tied itself to Iran’s fortunes. But while the Houthis are close to Iran, analysts describe their partnership as one shaped by both coordination and constraint.

Here’s what to know about the Houthis and their relationship with Iran.

The Houthis are Shiite militants who have been fighting Yemen’s internationally recognized government for about two decades. They overran the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014, forcing the government to flee to the southern city of Aden.

The following year, a Saudi-led coalition launched a bombing campaign to oust the militants but failed, leaving the Houthis in power in northern Yemen. Hundreds of thousands of people died from the violence, famine and disease that ensued in one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

The Houthis oppose Israel and the United States. The group is part of the so-called axis of resistance led by Iran, along with Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon and armed groups in Syria and Iraq.

Fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government subsided in recent years, and the United Nations helped broker a cease-fire in 2022.

Since then, the group has continued to launch attacks on its adversaries in the region. In the wake of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel that killed over 1,200 people and Israel’s subsequent bombardment of the Gaza Strip that has killed more than 73,000 people, the Houthis disrupted international shipping by firing on passing vessels in the Red Sea.

Crucial to the Houthis’ power is the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow waterway on Yemen’s southwest tip. The strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

Until recently, the Houthis’ involvement in the broader Iran war had been halting and cautious. Experts said the group had been weakened by last year’s weekslong bombardment by the United States and Israel in Yemen — and forced into a careful calculation about how much of its dwindling arsenal it could afford to spend.

The new front in the war started to crack open earlier this month, when Houthi authorities accused Saudi Arabia of attacking Yemen’s main international airport in Sanaa in a dispute over an Iranian plane that tried to land there.

Analysts say Iran may have also urged the Houthis to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea. With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed for months, the Red Sea has become a vital alternative export route for the transportation of Saudi oil and gas.

The Houthis are neither a direct conduit for Iranian interests in Yemen, nor a fully independent entity free of the Islamic Republic’s influence.

Analysts have said Iranian support helped the Houthis evolve from a group of poorly organized rebels to a powerful armed presence in the region, with an arsenal of cruise and ballistic missiles and long-range drones.

But the group has had to weigh its loyalty to Tehran alongside domestic calculations. It may have delayed engaging in full-scale confrontations in the current regional conflict because it could risk inviting renewed strikes on Houthi leadership and infrastructure — or even emboldening rival Yemeni factions.

item.title: Trump, His Money, and the World
item.description:
This summer, we learned that Donald Trump made at least $2.2 billion in his first year back in the White House. That’s a crazy amount of money. No other American president or leader of a liberal democracy has even come close to becoming so rich while in office.

And it comes with an unprecedented number of potential conflicts of interest, not just at home but also abroad, in countries with a much worse track record for good governance than the United States. Today, I write about how Trump’s global moneymaking enterprises risk empowering autocrats and seeding corruption around the world.

President Trump’s annual financial disclosure form gave my colleagues who scrutinize his finances a lot to work with.

I spoke with my colleague Eric Lipton, who covers the Trump family’s business operations. Throw a dart at the map, he suggested, and chances are it will land somewhere the American president or his family have business interests. As Eric has documented, Trump’s holding company last year collected at least $125 million in direct payments from foreign sources in countries including Britain, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Oman, the Philippines, Qatar, Romania, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Turkey, Vietnam and the United Arab Emirates.

Last year, an investment firm tied to the United Arab Emirates bought nearly half of the Trump family’s main cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial. Four months later, the Trump administration agreed to give the Emiratis access to sophisticated computer chips powering artificial intelligence.

Not long after, Trump got on the phone with the president of Kazakhstan to help a little-known American mining company win access to one of the world’s largest untapped reserves of tungsten, a critical metal. A short time later, Trump’s two eldest sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, became investors in a company that now owns a stake in that mining company.

The list goes on. Government officials in Vietnam fast-tracked a Trump golf development at the same time that they were trying to avoid steep U.S. tariffs. A South Korean company that has lobbied the U.S. to not impose penalties on its aluminum exports made a $2 million payment to Trump’s holding company for a golf course project. A drone maker backed by Trump’s two oldest sons is negotiating with Gulf countries that need to defend themselves because of a war started by their father.

Many have written about the potential impacts of these dealings on the U.S. itself — their effect on the rule of law, on public faith in government, on Trump’s ability to focus on the interests of the American people, rather than his own.

What might be going underappreciated is that they’re likely to have ripple effects around the world, too.

From enforcer to enabler

For a long time, the U.S. played a very different role: It was an enforcer of anti-corruption rules.

In 1977, after a series of scandals in which American companies secretly paid hundreds of millions of dollars in bribes to foreign officials, the U.S. passed the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. It threatens fines and even prison sentences for executives who pay officials overseas to win or keep business.

Then, the U.S. went even further, lobbying to have its anti-bribery standard adopted by more than 30 countries. U.S. regulators began rigorously enforcing the law against not just American companies, but any foreign corporation that used the U.S. financial system or markets.

The enforcement efforts “were so intense and the penalties so severe that international corporations really became quite concerned and adapted their practices,” Eric told me.

Under Trump, two things have shifted, Eric said. On the policy side, one of the first things Trump did after returning to the White House was to largely suspend the enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. The administration effectively turned a blind eye to bribes from American companies in the name of economic and national security, arguing that the law, as enforced, made it harder for U.S. companies to acquire critical assets like minerals and deepwater ports.

Then there are Trump’s own potential conflicts of interest. Combined, the two risk being read as a green light for pay-to-play schemes around the world.

(The White House says there are no conflicts of interest because Trump’s sons run the family business operations.)

It’s impossible to say how much this has increased corruption globally. Such schemes, by definition, tend to happen in secret, making them difficult to measure.

But “the United States, the cop on the block, has walked away,” Eric said. We might not know the degree to which that has affected corruption around the world — but we can make a pretty good guess at the direction.

Transactional, with a twist

Liz David-Barrett of Sussex University, who studies transnational corruption, told me that America’s relationship with the rest of the world has changed. Today, she said, it’s looking increasingly like Russia’s or China’s relationship with the world.

Russia and China have a track record of regularly investing in countries with poor governance.

Russia, for example, exploited corrupt governments in Serbia and Hungary to get investment deals in the state energy monopoly and key infrastructure projects. China has cut deals with repressive governments around the world to secure critical resources, including oil from Venezuela and lithium from Zimbabwe.

It’s a transactional, no-questions-asked model favored by countries that have lax labor and environmental rules, and leaders open to corruption. Most experts agree it helped prop up corrupt and authoritarian regimes, including those of Bashar al-Assad in Syria and Viktor Orban in Hungary.

Now, Trump is doing something that looks roughly the same, those experts say, but with a twist: He openly blurs the line between what’s in his country’s interest and what’s in his own interest.

That risks creating problems for America. But it might create problems for the rest of the world, too.

Trump put the newly signed U.S.-Saudi nuclear deal in doubt with a new condition: The kingdom must first establish diplomatic ties with Israel.

Iran rejected a cease-fire proposal from Trump that was carried to Tehran by the Iraqi prime minister, according to Iranian and Iraqi officials.

A Russian spy left Japan after his activities were revealed by The New York Times.

The European Union fined Google $1 billion for anti-competitive practices in its search engine.

A prominent Indian activist ended his hunger strike yesterday after 26 days fasting in solidarity with the country’s young protesters. See a defining image of the protests.

The influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate, who are being extradited to Britain on charges including human trafficking and rape, are losing the support of allies in Trump’s orbit.

The U.S. Justice Department withdrew subpoenas for New York Times journalists who reported on the security capabilities of Trump’s new Qatari-built Air Force One.

WHAT ELSE IS HAPPENING

Japanese authorities held a contest earlier this year to select a name for a day of temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius or higher. The winner was kokushobi, meaning “cruel heat day.” The term was used for the first time this week.

Four mathematicians were awarded the Fields Medal, which is given every four years to the brightest young researchers in the field.

TOP OF THE WORLD

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about the death of a man who introduced Jeffrey Epstein to young women.

You might have seen them on your feed: hyperrealistic ads promising medical miracles with plant-based pills and supplements. A Times analysis found campaigns by hundreds of A.I.-generated doctors, healers and wellness influencers on social media. Many appear to be targeting older women, while making misleading health claims for profit.

“I’ve had a hand in killing around six people. Maybe seven,” writes Thomas Gibbons-Neff, a a former U.S. Marine in Afghanistan who later became a Times journalist. “These decisions to pull the trigger were the final steps of our part in a strategy that was doomed before I even deployed.”

After covering several conflicts as a journalist, Thomas ultimately decided to leave The Times to become an English teacher. In May, during his final weeks at The Times, he returned to Afghanistan to speak with someone he once fought against: a Taliban commander. Here’s what he found.

The Louvre Museum’s Apollo Gallery is crammed with paintings, sculptures and tapestries. But earlier this week, when the gilded gallery opened for the first time in more than nine months, it felt strangely empty: The crown jewels, once a centerpiece of the room, were missing. They were stolen in October by burglars who made off with gems worth more than $100 million.

The museum visitors who returned to the room said they had been traumatized by the heist. “It was like a piece of myself was gone,” one said. “There is a void.” Read more about the missing jewels.

Bibingka is a Filipino cake traditionally made with rice flour and coconut milk that’s baked to supreme fluffiness over banana leaves in a terra-cotta oven. This version is built to fit in the palm of one’s hand. The final touch is macapuno — opalescent strands from rare, prized coconuts with jellylike flesh.

Can you guess this national park?

Kakadu, Australia

Everglades, U.S.

Pantanal Matogrossense, Brazil

Sundarbans, India

Interviewing Zohran Mamdani last week in New York was a big moment for the newsletter. (It also gave me a lot of street cred with my 14-year-old daughter and her friends.) I’d like to have more of these kinds of conversations, and to take The World into the room with me. So if there’s anyone you’d like to hear from — including anyone who is currently flying a little more under the radar — send me a note!

It’s interesting — at a time when people are turning away from national politics, recent polls show Mamdani has actually become more popular among New Yorkers. Those polls don’t say why, but many of the people I talked to told me stories of running into Mamdani around the city — out at a night club, or visiting a school, or even just walking around the streets of Queens.

There’s something intriguing here about local politics and the link mayors have with their voters that feels noteworthy in this polarized moment. Andy Burnham, the new British prime minister, is also a former mayor. I’m hoping to explore this in a future edition of The World.

But first — vacation! I’m off next week, and my holiday playlist is almost finished. (Don’t worry, the newsletter will go on without me.) The first song, and one that I have been playing on repeat for happy vibes, is “You Got the Love” by Rufus & Chaka Khan.

See you in August! — Katrin

Here are today’s Spelling Bee, Mini Crossword, Wordle and Sudoku. Find all our games here.

We welcome your feedback. Send us your suggestions at theworld@nytimes.com.

item.title: Senators Ask Hegseth to Fully Account for U.S. Troops Killed or Wounded in Iran
item.description:
Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee urged Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday to provide “a full and accurate accounting” of all U.S. troops killed or wounded in the Iran war.

“The information currently available to the public suggests that the department has not consistently provided timely and comprehensive public casualty reporting throughout the conflict,” Senator Mazie Hirono of Hawaii said in a letter also signed by the panel’s 11 other Democrats.

The senators said the Pentagon’s system for tracking casualties, which the Defense Department has said is updated regularly, has reported “inconsistent casualty figures, raising additional questions about the transparency and reliability of the department’s public reporting and statements.”

The Pentagon said earlier this week that roughly 100 American troops had been injured by Iranian attacks since early July. The Defense Department did not disclose the latest casualties in Jordan and elsewhere in the Middle East until The New York Times reported on injuries from four attacks last week, the last of which, on Friday, killed three soldiers and wounded several others.

At least 18 U.S. service members have died in the war since it started on Feb. 28, and about 570 have been wounded so far.

item.title: Iran Rejects U.S. Cease-Fire Deal Presented by Iraqi Leader
item.description:
Iran on Thursday rejected a cease-fire proposal from President Trump that was carried to Tehran by the Iraqi prime minister, according to Iranian and Iraqi officials. The failed mediation effort came as Mr. Trump was threatening to escalate the war and target Iran’s critical infrastructure.

The officials, who asked not to be identified because they were discussing sensitive national security issues, said Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s trip to Iran followed his recent visit with Mr. Trump at the White House.

The details of the cease-fire proposal were not immediately clear. But Iranian officials said that it was the only offer on the table, and that their government was not interested in a temporary deal that left the question of control over the Strait of Hormuz unresolved.

Mr. al-Zaidi traveled to Tehran with a delegation of senior Iraqi officials and met with President Masoud Pezeshkian; Iran’s top negotiator, Brig. Gen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf; and its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, according to local media reports.

Mr. Araghchi told state television that Iran and Iraq, which share a border, had mutual economic, political and security interests and close ties and that the visit was significant given the current circumstances in the region.

Mr. Araghchi said that Mr. al-Zaidi had shared his “views and impressions” from his trip to Washington, but that Tehran and Washington already had enough mediators. “The problem is not passing messages,” he said. “The problem is America’s outlook, which is illogical, greedy and controlling.”

Iran and the United States have steadily escalated tensions over the past few weeks, with American forces bombing military bases, as well as infrastructure like railroads, airports, bridges and seaports. Iran has launched strikes with ballistic missiles and drones on American military targets in the Middle East.

Two Iranian officials said that the country’s armed forces were anticipating — and preparing for — the possibility of the war expanding if Mr. Trump carries through with his threats to strike the capital of Tehran and critical infrastructure. If he does, the officials said, Iran will expand the fight regionally, including by striking Tel Aviv and asking its Houthi allies to close Bab al-Mandab, a strategic waterway in the Red Sea.

On Thursday in Tehran’s Azadi Square, where supporters of the government stage nightly pro-war rallies, a military vehicle paraded Iranian-made ballistic missiles pointing at the sky.

item.title: Prominent Indian Activist Breaks Hunger Strike After 26 Days
item.description:
A prominent Indian activist ended his hunger strike on Thursday after 26 days of fasting to demand the education minister’s resignation over a series of botched entrance exams. But India’s young protesters are continuing what has grown into a wider fight against corruption, poor job prospects and the government’s mismanagement of the education system.

The activist, Sonam Wangchuk, announced on social media that he had broken his fast “after long negotiations” with government ministers and “in view of possible violence in the country.” He had started striking in solidarity with a wider protest that began after India’s medical school entrance exams were canceled in May because test questions had been leaked.

The cause has since morphed into a wider Gen Z movement calling for structural changes to the education system and labor market, with thousands taking part in demonstrations in major Indian cities in recent days. In New Delhi, where the demonstrations began and have raged, and where young protesters were met on Monday by a heavy police response, anger against the government writ large has been intensifying.

The driving force behind the protests is the Cockroach Janta Party, a movement that is not a real political party and began as satire, taking its name from an insult. Its president, Abhijeet Dipke, said he was “relieved and grateful” that Mr. Wangchuk had ended his hunger strike. But he said the party’s peaceful protest would continue until the education minister resigns.

The party has called for nationwide rallies on Friday and said that protests had already spread to more than 30 Indian cities.

The Delhi police said its officers had moved Mr. Wangchuk, a longtime activist on education and climate issues, “to the hospital for essential medical care” in keeping with court orders. As Mr. Wangchuk’s health deteriorated there, government ministers urged him to break his fast.

Yet there was no indication that the government had agreed to meet any of the demands driving Mr. Wangchuk’s strike. Chief among them was the resignation of the Indian education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, under whose watch a number of national exams have been marred by leaks. Mr. Wangchuck has also called on the government to vow not to punish protesters.

Mr. Wangchuck said he would offer an explanation for why he broke his fast in a video that would be published later. He urged “all to stay very vigilant about not allowing violence of any kind anywhere.”

Many of the protesters in India are students, and many others have jobs, but they share a sense of desperation and rage about education and employment prospects. As the movement spreads across the country, these young people are posing one of the most substantial challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his 12 years in power.

item.title: A Russian Spy, Suddenly Cast Into the Spotlight, Flees Japan
item.description:
A Russian spy at the center of a secret operation to smuggle high-tech weapon components into Russia has left Japan after his activities were disclosed by The New York Times, a senior Ukrainian intelligence official said on Thursday.

The operative, Maksim Vladimirovich Filchenkov, 49, had been working undercover in Japan as an employee of the Russian state airline Aeroflot. Mr. Filchenkov’s role had been the focus of a Times investigation into how Russia exploited Japan’s weak espionage laws.

Mr. Filchenkov’s departure was first reported by Yomiuri Shimbun, a major national newspaper in Japan. The newspaper said the Russian exited Japan after The Times published its investigation on July 12. The Ukrainian official who confirmed the spy’s departure did so on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss intelligence publicly.

The Russian spy’s presence in that country had frustrated Ukraine, which had repeatedly warned that, despite Japan’s export restrictions and economic sanctions, its high-tech components were still being shipped to Russia. Ninety percent of Russian missiles and drones contain Japanese components, according to Ukrainian government estimates.

“This is definitely good news and it’s an important example of what has to be done,” said Sergiy Korsunsky, who served as Ukraine’s ambassador to Japan from 2020 to 2024. He said he had raised concerns with Japanese officials about their technology finding its way to the battlefield.

Mr. Filchenkov was part of a clandestine unit known as the 20th Directorate of Russia’s military intelligence agency, the G.R.U. Posing as diplomats or businesspeople, its officers work to buy or steal battlefield technology and smuggle it into Russia.

That made Mr. Filchenkov, a veteran officer who had previously served in Japan, a key cog in supplying Russia’s war machine as he formed business relationships with logistics companies that ship goods from Japan to Russia, often through intermediary countries.

Mr. Filchenkov has not responded to messages seeking comment. He declined to meet with reporters who visited the Aeroflot office earlier this year.

Former intelligence officials familiar with Russian intelligence operations say that spies whose identities have been revealed often return to Moscow and work desk jobs or train future generations of spies — meaning Mr. Filchenkov’s undercover days are likely over. But officials say that the 20th Directorate remains a key part of the Kremlin’s effort to obtain weapons components.

The Japanese government has not directly addressed questions about him or the 20th Directorate but said that the Times report showed the need to better combat foreign espionage. Minoru Kihara, a top Japanese cabinet official, said the country “must address this issue with even greater rigor.”

Japan is working to build an intelligence agency, which it has not had since World War II. The country has also backed Ukraine in its devastating war with Russia, which has inflicted heavy casualties on both sides. Immediately after Russia’s invasion, Japan, along with the United States and the European Union, imposed economic sanctions.

Japan later began sending military aid like bulletproof vests and helmets to Ukraine, breaking with post-World War II precedent. And in May, Japan began sending personnel to NATO Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine, a team that coordinates security support for Ukraine.

In an interview, Mr. Korsunsky said that Russia began stockpiling Japanese technology shortly before it invaded Ukraine, placing big orders with Japanese manufacturers around 2021.

In the early days of the war, Ukrainian investigators recovered weapons parts mostly from China and Iran. But as the war shifted from artillery battles to drone warfare, they started discovering more Japanese technology in Russian weapons.

“While I was in office, several times we transferred information we received from our authorities in Ukraine to Japanese authorities about its technology being found in drones and rockets,” said Mr. Korsunsky. “It was clear that the channels to supply all those spare parts were not closed.”

Indeed, after a Russian cruise missile destroyed a residential building in Kyiv and killed at least 24 people in May, investigators found that the missile had been guided by Japanese components — ones widely banned from export to Russia, according to a Ukrainian assessment.

item.title: Why Jordan Hosts U.S. Troops Even as That Makes It a Target
item.description:
For some three decades, Jordan has been an important base for American military operations around the Middle East.

Now, Jordan is paying a price. Over recent days, Iran has stepped up its airstrikes against the kingdom, targeting U.S. military forces there.

But even as sirens are sounding over Jordan, it has refrained from limiting the American presence. The country’s exceptional dependence on the United States has kept Jordan from curtailing those military activities, analysts say.

Jordan has come to rely on the United States for billions of dollars in economic and military aid, provided over their decades-old relationship, as well as for protection in a dangerous region.

Unlike some of its Gulf Arab neighbors with abundant oil and other natural resources, Jordan is a resource-poor country heavily reliant on foreign aid. Last year, the United States gave the kingdom $1.65 billion in economic and military assistance, according to Jordanian officials.

And while some other American allies in the region have restricted Washington’s ability to base troops on their territory and fly aircraft over it during the war with Iran, U.S. officials say, Jordan is not in a position to place such limits.

“Jordan is a weak state in the Middle East,” said Sean Yom, a professor of political science at Temple University and author of the book “Jordan: Politics in an Accidental Crucible.” “It’s fairly small and it’s surrounded by regional threats. And it does need some sort of great power patron or outside protector, and the U.S. has played that role for several generations now.”

The assistance Jordan gets from the United States, which dates back to the 1950s, is far too large for anyone else to provide, Mr. Yom said.

Since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran in late February, it has retaliated in part by carrying out strikes on American allies in the Middle East. During the first months of the war, Iran primarily targeted Israel and U.S. allies in the Gulf, but it also directed hundreds of drones and missiles at Jordan.

The conflict quickly hurt Jordan’s tourism industry, which provides up to 18 percent of the country’s revenue, just as the high season was getting underway. Although most of the missiles and drones were intercepted, airlines canceled flights, and would-be visitors canceled hotel reservations.

Now, with the U.S.-Iran cease-fire unraveling, both sides have ramped up attacks, and Iran has widened its targeting in recent weeks. On Sunday, Jordan’s air defenses shot down three Iranian missiles, the Jordanian military said, while a fourth landed in an unpopulated area.

“This Iranian strategy of vertical escalation hitting its neighbors aims at creating pressure on those neighbors, aims at creating pressure on the United States,” said Hassan Almomani, director of the Center for Strategic Studies, a think tank that advises the Jordanian government on national security.

Iran said recently that some of its strikes on Jordan had targeted fuel tanks at the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Azraq, a hub for the U.S. Air Force, and aircraft shelters at other bases, according to the Fars News Agency, a semiofficial Iranian news outlet. Previously, Iran said it had targeted radar and communications systems used by U.S. forces.

Three U.S. soldiers were killed on Friday in an Iranian attack on the Muwaffaq Salti base. Three other attacks on U.S. forces in Jordan earlier in the week wounded dozens of American soldiers and damaged a number of Blackhawk helicopters.

American forces have long operated out of Jordanian air bases, and the kingdom has been a base for such American military activities as the fight against the Islamic State, the training of rebel fighters during Syria’s civil war and the invasion of Iraq. There are now nearly 4,000 American service members in the country, according to a congressional report.

Muwaffaq Salti and other bases have been adapted to accommodate a permanent U.S. presence.

“The infrastructure in Jordan has been pretty robust from a U.S. standpoint for a while,” said Grant Rumley, a former Middle East adviser at the Pentagon and now a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. He likened it to a “land-based aircraft carrier.”

Muwaffaq Salti is also relatively remote, allowing U.S. forces to operate without attracting unwanted attention, Mr. Rumley said. And since Jordan is farther from Iran than Gulf countries, U.S. forces in Jordan have more time to respond to missile and drone attacks, he said.

In the run-up to the war with Iran and in its early days, the U.S. military moved some of its troops from several Gulf Arab nations to relatively more secure locations in Jordan and neighboring Israel, U.S. officials said.

“War in Iran has revealed how important Jordan is to the United States,” said Mr. Almomani. This year, he said, Washington has increased military aid to Jordan by half a billion dollars.

Jordanian officials often emphasize the strategic importance of their relationship with the United States. In a call with President Trump in April, King Abdullah II stressed Washington’s pivotal role in the Middle East, specifically in prospects for de-escalating the conflict with Iran.

Earlier this month, Jordan’s army chief, Maj. Gen. Yousef Hunaiti, and the U.S. assistant secretary of defense for international security affairs, Daniel Zimmerman, discussed expanding military cooperation further, according to the Petra state news agency in Jordan.

The Jordanian government rarely discusses the extensive U.S. military presence publicly. Nor has Jordan openly criticized the U.S. for its airstrikes on Iran or for launching the war alongside Israel, though analysts say that the government was strongly opposed to the conflict from the beginning.

Jordanian officials have repeatedly condemned Iran’s attacks on its soil, and last week Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi said the Iranian justification for its strikes — that there are U.S. bases — is false.

“There are no American bases in Jordan,” he said, speaking at a panel discussion at the Aspen Security Forum. “We have American troops that are in Jordan as part of our longstanding military cooperation. Their presence is governed by a defense agreement that fully respects our sovereignty.”

Despite the attacks, Jordan would not consider re-evaluating its alliance with the U.S., Mr. Almomani said. “Under no circumstances can Jordan change its strategic partnership,” he said.

There is no meaningful demand in Jordan for giving up its dependency on the United States, Mr. Yom said.

“No serious political stakeholder is suggesting that Jordan replace over $1.5 billion in economic and military assistance it receives from the United States every year with, say, European Union money or Chinese support,” he said.

Aaron Boxerman contributed reporting from Jerusalem.

item.title: Zelensky’s Dizzying U-Turn Is the Latest Zigzag in a Presidency Full of Them
item.description:
Before he became president, Volodymyr Zelensky played Napoleon in a comedic film that portrayed his character as a headstrong idiot who refused to change course even as he led his army to ruin.

As president, Mr. Zelensky has been the opposite of his depiction of the French general — being, perhaps, flexible to a fault. He has so often reversed decisions on appointments and policies that confusion and personnel churn are risks in his wartime leadership, analysts say.

In the latest turmoil, over the past week and a half, Mr. Zelensky sided at first with a seasoned commanding general in a dispute with a popular, reformist defense minister over military strategy and what weapons to buy. He dismissed the minister last week. Then, late Tuesday, he fired the general and appointed in his place a military chief a generation younger who is allied with the defense minister just ousted.

It was a head-scratching reversal that Mr. Zelensky did not explain publicly, other than to affirm his commitment to overhauls aimed at strengthening the army.

The episode has left Ukraine in the grips of some of the worst turbulence in domestic politics since Russia’s all-out invasion in 2022. Protesters have taken to the streets in anger over the dismissal of the defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, and Mr. Zelensky’s latest about-face has not quelled calls for further demonstrations.

To Mr. Zelensky’s allies, his willingness to listen to public opinion and make U-turns is a sign of the strength of Ukrainian democracy and an important contrast with autocratic Russian governance. Nearly four and a half years into the war, and seven years into his presidency, a majority of Ukrainians say they trust Mr. Zelensky as a leader.

But his frequent swerves can project weakness as the crucible of war demands steadfast leadership. One criticism of Mr. Zelensky is that he has carried his show business instincts into politics, playing for the loudest applause and zigzagging in search of approval.

“The good news is, he course-corrects,” said Orysia Lutsevych, head of the Ukraine program at Chatham House in London.

The bad news, she added, is how often and blatantly he does it. “He bends. He has some doubts as a person. He is unsure of himself,” Ms. Lutsevych said.

After firing Mr. Fedorov, Mr. Zelensky turned around and offered him other jobs in the government. On Thursday, after days of speculation over whether Mr. Fedorov would agree to a new appointment, he said in a statement that he would accept only an offer to return as defense minister.

“No other role,” he said, “carries the actual authority” to fight corruption in weapons purchases, modernize the army and finish other initiatives that the defense ministry had started during his brief six-month tenure.

Mr. Zelensky has signaled that he will nominate another candidate to be defense minister. If he sticks with that plan, one risk to Mr. Zelensky is that Mr. Fedorov will emerge as a potential political opponent.

In his U-turn on military leadership, Mr. Zelensky has not openly conceded an error. At a closed-door meeting with members of his political party last week, he described a quandary in the clash between his defense minister and his top general, Oleksandr Syrskyi, according to Ukrainian news media.

Mr. Fedorov, an evangelist for automated weaponry, had accused General Syrskyi of stalling robotization strategies. Mr. Zelensky told his political allies that he had considered resolving the rift by firing both men but worried about overly abrupt changes in leadership, according to the news reports. So he dismissed only the minister, signaling that he had sided with the general.

Before Russia’s invasion, Mr. Zelensky’s government was a revolving door. He began his presidency with an ambitious agenda of privatizing agricultural land and overhauling governance of state-owned enterprises. But he ousted his first cabinet after less than a year.

At one point during the Covid-19 pandemic, he replaced his health minister twice in one month.

In the first years after the all-out invasion, Mr. Zelensky left in place most key ministers and security service leaders. But a government reshuffle he initiated this month, which included his removal of Mr. Fedorov, is the second in a year.

And last summer, Mr. Zelensky made another switchback, on his government’s plan to weaken anticorruption agencies. He and his party’s lawmakers enacted the changes and then, amid mass demonstrations, reversed course.

Some appointments in his government overhaul this month stuck and generated little controversy.

Mr. Zelensky replaced Yuliia Svyrydenko, an economist, with Serhiy Koretsky, a former energy executive, as prime minister. The move was seen as preparation for expected Russian wintertime attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid.

But a major question remains over whether Mr. Zelensky will ultimately reverse himself completely by restoring Mr. Fedorov as defense minister. Doing so, said Volodymyr Fesenko, head of Penta, an independent analytical group in Kyiv, would weaken Mr. Zelensky’s position.

“If Fedorov returns to the post of defense minister in the current situation, a parallel power center will emerge in Ukraine,” Mr. Fesenko said. “This will be the beginning of Zelensky’s political end.”

item.title: ‘We Will All Die From Ebola Here’: Virus Stalks Crowded Camps in Congo
item.description:
Four deaths happened in just 24 hours.

The families were told they needed to bury the bodies themselves. Workers at the morgue were too busy to help. Nineteen people had already died in the camp that month, many more than usual.

Here in the camps dotted around Ituri Province, the epicenter of the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus appears to be spreading among the cramped tents that house more than a million displaced Congolese.

Despite an influx of aid and health workers since the outbreak was first officially declared in May, the battle against Ebola remains a staggering challenge, and the camps are a stark example. Sanitary conditions are dire. Access to basic nutrition is limited. Patients vanish down winding alleys. Tracing people who may be infected is a Sisyphean task.

With the death toll from Ebola skyrocketing in Congo, attention has turned to these camps, where some of the country’s most vulnerable people live after fleeing violence elsewhere in the Ituri Province. More than 80 percent of new Ebola cases in eastern Congo are being detected outside known contact lists, World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said this month.

Many of the new infections are happening in communities where people have little to no access to health facilities — communities like these camps.

Recent strikes by unpaid health workers, attacks on Ebola treatment centers and highly mobile populations have made matters worse. Congo’s health ministry has recorded 2,423 confirmed Ebola cases and 967 confirmed deaths as of this week. The W.H.O. has said the real numbers may be two to four times higher.

By far the biggest problem in the camps is the severe lack of water, according to officials at two different camps in the province. It makes one of the central pillars of fighting Ebola — proper sanitation to halt the spread of the disease — next to impossible.

One camp, called Kigonze, is home to 20,000 and only a handful of communal water stations. Residents stack yellow containers while waiting their turn at the spigot.

At the Tsere camp in Rwampara, just outside Bunia, the provincial capital, more than 6,400 people share a single water tank. Latrines overflowing with feces have not been maintained since they were built in 2023, residents said.

“During Ebola, we need to wash our hands all the time to avoid contamination,” said camp president Esther Mave. “But how can we do that here when we don’t have taps and sinks and soap?”

The lack of sanitation in the camps is in part due to the recent foreign aid cuts under President Trump. Data compiled by the United Nations showed that funding for toilets and hand-washing stations in Congo was cut by more than half between 2024 and 2025.

At least 55 people had already died in Kigonze between early April and late June, according to Etienne Dz’Djo Ndrutsi, the site’s president, who added that the camp usually averaged just two deaths per month. At least four of those deaths were confirmed Ebola cases, he added. But many more families had declined testing for lack of trust in the authorities after years of neglect.

“We need more beds to put all the dead bodies,” Mr. Ndrutsi said. “I’m afraid we will all die from Ebola here in this camp.”

Dozens of women and children recently crowded together under a corrugated metal roof of a building made from sticks and mud as they pressed against the coffins of three people who had died in the past 24 hours at Kigonze.

The dead — two men and a woman — had all shown symptoms of Ebola, including fever, headaches and vomiting, but swabs taken from their corpses had yet to be tested for the virus, which is highly infectious in dead bodies.

Women stroked the caskets as they sang and wept. Hundreds more swarmed the coffins as they were carried past makeshift shelters. Crowds then clambered onto a truck transporting the bodies for burial. Mourners sat atop the caskets while children ran behind the truck as it bounced along the road toward the cemetery.

Camp residents are displaced from their homes because of decades of violence between rival ethnic militias and armed groups vying for land, control of lucrative trade routes and access to gold and timber.

For residents, Ebola is just another threat.

Renewed fighting in Ituri has displaced 361,000 people since December, bringing the total number of displaced in the province to 1.3 million, according to the U.N. Insecurity has also hampered humanitarian efforts in the region.

“When there are clashes, children have been shot and killed in the crossfire. Another picked up an explosive and was killed,” Ms. Mave said.

Dr. Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said that the response to the outbreak needed to address more than just the health crisis to effectively reach people in the camps.

“The humanitarian response is critical today, as important as the health response,” he said. “Because we will not defeat this Ebola outbreak without dealing with the humanitarian issue.”

As international aid has arrived, camp residents who languished for years with little outside help have looked on skeptically. The contrast is stark at Tsere, located 200 yards from a new clinic run by the medical charity Alima.

“We can see them building an Ebola treatment center across the street, but they haven’t done anything here yet,” said Baudouin Unega, a 74-year-old camp resident. “They come, they do investigations, then they go away. They tell us there is no more funding, just to be patient.”

Camp residents work as laborers on local farms and sell firewood, but even that lifeline has frayed during the epidemic. Many local farmers have fled the virus, leaving the displaced with even fewer sources of income. “We want to leave the camp,” Mr. Unega said. “Nobody wants to live here, but there are no funds for us to leave.”

As he spoke, the Tsere camp recorded another death. Espérance Raciu Ucwimungu, 40, died of Ebola-like symptoms on a recent afternoon. Her sister Chantal Imani, 32, and daughter, Wivine Biwiga, 23, grieved outside the one-room hut they had shared with Ms. Ucwimungu.

Despite deplorable conditions and the fear of Ebola hanging over the camps, life goes on. Children chase each other through narrow alleyways. Markets do a brisk trade in basic goods. Women wash laundry and braid each other’s hair in the shade.

On the evening of the recent funerals in Kigonze, 18-year-old Isaak Dieume pressed a worn trumpet to his lips. Children gathered around, and women preparing a meal nearby looked on as he played a gentle tune.

Crisp notes hung in the air, their metallic sound offering a moment of joy on an afternoon of sorrow and loss.

Caleb Kabanda contributed reporting.
